topic: The Bridge Between Slopes and Areas: Understanding the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
target_audience: High school seniors or early university students

sections.title: Introduction: The Inverse Relationship
sections.content: Introduce the concept that differentiation and integration are inverse operations, much like addition and subtraction. Use a character-driven scenario to set the stage for why we need to connect 'rate of change' with 'accumulation'.
sections.example: Meet 'Dash the Cheetah'. If we know Dash's position at every second, we can find his speed (derivative). Conversely, if we only know his speed, can we find how far he traveled? This section introduces the 'Backwards' puzzle.

sections.title: Prerequisite Refresher: Slopes and Areas
sections.content: Quickly review the graphical meaning of the two concepts. Derivative = Slope of the tangent line at a point. Integral = Signed area under the curve between two points. This establishes the visual foundation.
sections.example: Visualizing a linear graph f(x) = 2x. Show the slope is a constant '2', and the area under the line forms a triangle, which grows as x increases.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
sections.content: Define a new function, A(x), which represents the area under a curve f(t) from a fixed point 'a' to a moving point 'x'. This is the 'Area-so-far' function. Use animation to show the area 'filling up' as x moves to the right.
sections.example: Imagine a snowblower clearing a path. The amount of snow collected (A(x)) depends on how far the snowblower has moved (x) and the height of the snow pile (f(x)) at that exact spot.

sections.title: The 'Aha!' Moment: The Rate of Area Growth
sections.content: Explain the core of the Fundamental Theorem: The rate at which the area A(x) grows is exactly equal to the height of the function f(x) at that point. Mathematically: A'(x) = f(x). This links the derivative of the integral back to the original function.
sections.example: A growing rectangle animation: As we increase the width by a tiny sliver 'dx', the change in area is roughly height times width [f(x) * dx]. Therefore, the change in area divided by change in x is just the height, f(x).

sections.title: Application: Speedometers and Odometers
sections.content: Apply the theory to a real-world device to solidify understanding. Show how the Fundamental Theorem allows us to calculate total change by evaluating the antiderivative at the endpoints.
sections.example: A car's dashboard: The Speedometer shows the derivative (velocity). The Odometer shows the integral (total distance). If you integrate the speedometer's reading over time, you get the change in the odometer's reading.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap that differentiation 'breaks down' a function to find its slope, while integration 'builds up' a function to find its area. The Fundamental Theorem is the bridge that proves these two processes are two sides of the same coin.
sections.example: A split-screen animation showing a function being differentiated on the left and an area being integrated on the right, ending with the 'Equal' sign connecting them through the Fundamental Theorem.
